Project Overview

The Statutory Credit Report landing page is a high-traffic entry point for users requiring legal access to their credit data. Despite its importance, the legacy page suffered from significant structural and strategic friction:

  • Visual Trust Deficit: An outdated interface that failed to meet modern FinTech aesthetics, reducing user confidence.
  • Information Scarcity: A lack of educational content regarding the service’s purpose, legal standing, and consumer benefits.
  • Under-Optimised Conversion Path: A weak value proposition and unclear messaging that left users hesitant to proceed.
  • Technical Debt: Poor mobile responsiveness and layout shifts that hindered the experience for the growing mobile-first demographic.

Objective

The primary goal was to re-engineer the landing page to harmonise UX best practices with aggressive SEO requirements, ultimately driving higher organic traffic and improving conversion rates (CRO).

Step 1: Research and Discovery

I conducted a multi-layered audit to ensure the redesign was rooted in data rather than just aesthetics. This involved bridging the gap between what users search for and what they need once they arrive.

Strategic Techniques

  1. Search Intent & Keyword Intelligence: I identified high-value clusters such as "statutory credit report" and "free credit report UK" to align the on-page copy with actual user mental models and search patterns.
  2. Competitive Benchmarking: Analysed the landscape to identify where competitors were outperforming Equifax in terms of content depth and "trust signals."
  3. SEO Gap Analysis: Evaluated the technical "under-the-hood" elements including metadata hierarchy, H-tag structures, and image alt-text to prepare for a developer-ready handoff.
  4. Qualitative Feedback Loop: Reviewed user pain points to identify common points of confusion during the initial discovery phase.

Key Findings

  • Cognitive Load: Users found it difficult to differentiate the Statutory Report from subscription-based products.
  • CTA Friction: The "Call to Action" buttons lacked visual weight and persuasive micro-copy.
  • Mobile Failure: Core elements were breaking on smaller viewports, leading to high bounce rates.
  • Organic Invisibility: Missing keyword integration meant the page was failing to capture "top-of-funnel" organic traffic.

Step 2: Defining Design & Growth Goals

The research phase informed a roadmap focused on three pillars: Design, Conversion, and Performance.

  1. Establish Authority: Modernise the visual language to reflect Equifax’s position as a global data leader.
  2. Information Architecture: Use progressive disclosure to organise complex regulatory information into digestible modules.
  3. CRO Optimisation: Implement high-contrast, action-oriented CTAs designed to reduce pogo-sticking and increase click-through rates.
  4. Performance & SEO: Architect the page with a "Mobile-First" mindset, ensuring clean code structures for optimal search engine crawling.

Step 3: Design & Interaction Logic

UX and CRO Highlights

  • Strategic Visual Hierarchy: I prioritised the most critical information at the top of the page, ensuring the value proposition is visible within the first three seconds of the user landing.
  • Trust Signals: Introduced iconography and structured infographics to break up dense text, improving the readability and "skim-ability" of the page.
  • Conversion-Centred Design: Buttons were redesigned with accessible, high-contrast colours and "active" verb-based labels to trigger user intent.
  • Semantic HTML Structure: From a developer perspective, I organised the content using a strict H1 through H3 hierarchy. This not only aids accessibility (screen readers) but provides clear signals to Google regarding content relevancy.

Proposed Design

Registration Flow Optimisation

Beyond the landing page, I mapped out recommendations for the registration journey to ensure the conversion momentum wasn't lost at the first form field.

Step 4: Technical Validation

To ensure the design would perform in a live environment, I conducted several validation exercises:

  1. Usability Testing: Evaluated the prototype’s navigation flow to ensure users could find the "Start" button without hesitation.
  2. Hotspot Analysis: Verified that visual attention was being successfully directed toward the primary CTAs and key benefit statements.
  3. Technical SEO Audit: Validated the proposed metadata and schema structure against industry-standard SEO requirements.

Step 5: Challenges and Performance Limitations

Challenges

  • Regulatory Constraints: Balancing marketing-led CRO with the strict legal wording required for statutory reporting was a primary challenge.
  • Technical Constraints: As this was a UX-led proposal, I focused on solutions that could be implemented via standard CMS components without requiring custom heavy engineering.

Limitations

  • This project was a dedicated UX performance test. While prototypes showed significant improvement in user understanding, the results are based on simulated validation rather than live A/B testing data.

Step 6: Conclusion

This case study highlights my ability to act as a bridge between Design, SEO, and Development. By treating a landing page as a functional product rather than a static document, I was able to:

  • Enhance Search Visibility: Integrating data-driven keywords into a semantically correct structure.
  • Improve User Experience: Solving mobile responsiveness and accessibility issues that directly impact the bottom line.
  • Drive Business Value: Redesigning the conversion funnel to turn passive visitors into active applicants.

This project reinforces my core strength: using deep research and technical SEO knowledge to build visually compelling, high-performing digital experiences that align with both user needs and business KPIs.
